section.title: Introduction
section.para: A glossary maps surface forms, including multiword terms, to stable identifiers. The package opennlp.tools.glossary compiles a list of GlossaryEntry values into an AhoCorasickGlossaryMatcher. Use GlossaryAnnotator to add the matches to a document. Results contain the registered identifier, term, and span in the original text.

section.title: Matching through a pipeline
section.para: The annotator requires no input layers. This example combines glossary matching with a model-free tokenizer in a DocumentAnalyzer. The glossary layer is GlossaryAnnotator.GLOSSARY; token annotations remain available separately. Case-insensitive matching accepts capitalization differences without changing the source offsets.

After annotation, the glossary layer is present even when no matches are found. Before annotation, get(GlossaryAnnotator.GLOSSARY) returns an empty list but layers() does not contain the key. An existing glossary layer is rejected before the matcher runs. Combine matchers in one annotator when they contribute to the same output layer.

section.title: Matching with an offset-aware normalizer
section.para: The two-argument matcher compares characters literally, aside from the optional per-code-point case fold. Length-changing orthographic folds such as German umlaut expansion, full Unicode case folding, whitespace collapse, or dash folding are supplied through the three-argument constructor that takes a non-null OffsetAwareNormalizer. Terms and text are normalized before matching, and result spans map back to the original text. Use TermAnalyzingGlossaryMatcher for token-level stemming.

A custom aligned normalizer may insert text without consuming source characters. A match covering only inserted text has a zero-length source span. Overlap selection follows Span.intersects, including for such spans; a zero-length span intersects a span containing that offset, including the end offset.

section.title: Matching inflected forms through TermAnalyzer
section.para: Token-level inflection needs a stemmer. Build a TermAnalyzingGlossaryMatcher over a TermAnalyzer that case-folds and stems. The matcher runs Aho-Corasick over normalized tokens and reports spans from the first matched token's original start to the last matched token's original end, so a registered hot dog covers the surface hot dogs. Use AhoCorasickGlossaryMatcher for exact and orthographic matching when no tokenizer is required.

The word tokenizer excludes punctuation, so the characters between consecutive tokens do not take part in matching: hot-dogs, hot, dogs, and hot. Dogs all match a registered hot dog, with the span covering the separators between the matched tokens. Process individual sentences when matches must not span sentence boundaries. Tokens that normalize to blank are omitted during input matching, but a registered term containing such a token is rejected. A lemmatizing analyzer is rejected at construction because this matcher does not supply POS tags.

A whole-text OffsetAwareNormalizer can run before tokenization. This is required for a transform that changes one source token into multiple tokens, such as English contraction expansion. The three-argument matcher constructor applies the transform to both registered terms and source text, then maps matched tokens back to source offsets. Ambiguous contractions are preserved. Quoted contractions expand, but fragments inside longer words or identifiers do not.

section.title: Combining matchers with CompositeGlossaryMatcher
section.para: Use CompositeGlossaryMatcher to combine exact and inflected matches in a single GlossaryAnnotator. List order determines priority: a match is accepted only if it does not overlap an accepted match. Placing the exact matcher before the inflected matcher gives exact matches priority. Adjacent non-empty spans are accepted, and results are returned in text order. Custom delegates must return sorted, non-overlapping matches, as required by GlossaryMatcher.

section.title: Matching in unspaced CJK text
section.para: Word boundaries follow the complete default rules in UAX #29. This includes apostrophes, combining marks, variation selectors, connector punctuation, emoji ZWJ sequences, and supplementary-plane characters. Han ideographs and hiragana receive character-granularity boundaries, so glossary terms match inside unspaced Chinese and Japanese text without configuring a tokenizer. Spans refer to the original characters. An English contraction is a single word segment, so can does not match inside can't.

The default UAX #29 rules define locale-neutral boundaries, not linguistic word segmentation. Katakana and Hangul runs stay joined, and scripts such as Thai, Lao, Khmer, and Myanmar need dictionary-based tailoring when callers require language-specific words. The TermAnalyzingGlossaryMatcher uses these boundaries too: both matcher types use WordSegmenter.

section.title: Loading glossaries from TBX and CSV files
section.para: The opennlp.tools.formats.glossary package in opennlp-formats loads TBX, CSV, and TSV files. TbxGlossaryReader accepts TBX 2 and TBX 3 element names; CsvGlossaryReader loads delimited term lists. Both return GlossaryEntry values in file order. Aliases use the same identifier in multiple entries. GlossaryLoadingExampleTest verifies the examples below.

The TBX reader selects a language at construction, ignoring case and accepting additional subtags: en selects en-US, but en-GB does not select en-US. A DOCTYPE is accepted and internal entities are expanded. External DTD content is not loaded. External entity declarations, including unused ones, are rejected with InvalidFormatException, as are missing unqualified id attributes, blank selected terms, and malformed XML.

Term extraction follows text/body, then a concept entry, a language section, and a term container. Containers are tig or ntig/termGrp in TBX 2 and termSec in TBX 3. Header, back-matter, and metadata subtrees are ignored, even when they contain elements named term. Inline text inside a selected term is retained. This reader extracts terms; it does not validate the complete TBX schema.

Structural elements must use the namespace urn:iso:std:iso:30042:ed-2 or no namespace. Namespace prefixes are accepted. Extension fields in other namespaces are ignored, including fields with names such as term or termSec.

Both readers leave the supplied stream open on success or failure. Close it after use, as in this example. Input I/O failures propagate as IOException; invalid file content is reported as InvalidFormatException.

The CSV reader takes the delimiter and header convention explicitly: the first column is the identifier, the next is the term, and additional column values are ignored. Quoting follows RFC 4180: quoted fields may contain delimiters, doubled quotes, and line breaks. Unquoted fields cannot contain quotes. After a closing quote, only a delimiter, record end, or input end is accepted. These checks also apply to headers and ignored columns.

CSV input must be valid UTF-8; a leading byte order mark is removed. Malformed encoded characters produce InvalidFormatException instead of replacement characters. LF, CRLF, and CR record separators are supported. Blank lines are skipped. Errors in quoting, missing columns, and blank identifiers or terms include physical line numbers, accounting for line breaks inside quoted fields.

section.title: English contractions
section.para: English contraction expansion is opt-in. A supported contraction must occupy a complete word under the default UAX #29 word boundaries.
